### 安全/漏洞

- [「我们可能会失去公钥密码学」：Green 那条推文背后到底在说什么](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_green-public-key-cryptography-ai/): Full translation of the 15-tweet clarification thread Matthew Green (Johns Hopkins) posted on 8 October 2026 after a casual reply tweet of his ('I think we might lose public key cryptography', clarified as 'well, encryption specifically') was widely reshared. Covers his opening warning against overreaction (don't stop using TLS, don't post Bitcoin seeds in cleartext, don't start treating Telegram as a secure messenger - 'encryption is good, use it'), his explicit statement that he knows of no imminent cryptanalysis results and his inference from the questions being asked about which frontier labs probably do not have one, and the precise scope of his concern: not public-key cryptography in principle and not all of it, but standardized public-key encryption and some signatures, specifically because most of it rests on a small number of hard problems - currently essentially MLWE and ECDLP, with LWE and syndrome decoding as backups. Sets out his central argument: these problems were extensively analysed by humans and we felt confident that the best known attacks were the best attacks, but we are learning that human mathematical analysis is not the gold standard; the optimistic view that we got it all right is 'a very opinionated bet', and opinionated bets are not safe when global Internet security is at stake. Explains what losing public-key encryption would mean - not that encryption becomes impossible or that we live in Minicrypt, but that new cryptanalytic results substantially improve attacks on standardized schemes, with the milder effect being that schemes thought to offer 128-bit security are really 96 or 108 bits, forcing honest standards bodies to deprecate at least the smaller parameter sets already deployed in live systems. Then the crux: crank parameters up to what, when current numbers rest on 40 (or 25) years of human study and we could be off by 26 bits; the fallback would be trusting that the machines say they are stuck, which he says nobody will feel good about, especially if a new internal model makes another step-change jump, leaving trust only at painfully high security levels. Adds the trigger context the Chinese discussion omits: OpenAI's release of 722 AI-generated mathematical papers (grouped into about 372, roughly 4,000 problems fed in, about 5 percent success rate) that Scott Aaronson called the 'Mathocalypse', three papers withdrawn on 7 October over a sign error in a Weil-classes proof, and criticism from Terence Tao and the Association for Human Mathematicians. Covers the industry reaction (Ethereum researcher Justin Drake urging 'bunker mode' preparation, Vitalik Buterin arguing AI may threaten cryptocurrency more than quantum computers and that lattices will need to be significantly bigger, plus his advice to hold funds in addresses whose public keys have not yet been exposed) and the crucial caveat that no evidence shows OpenAI's results come close to defeating deployed cryptography, and that the correctness of the proofs is itself unverified. Closes by noting his prior posts (July on Anthropic's Claude Mythos attack on HAWK reducing effective key recovery from 2^64 to 2^38 and improved reduced-round AES attacks, and August on software going 'dark'), and by separating technical risk from the epistemic risk that we lose the ability to know how safe we are.
  - Key topics: Matthew Green, public key cryptography, MLWE, ECDLP, LWE, syndrome decoding, lattice cryptography, parameter sizes, 128-bit security level, standards bodies, deprecation, Minicrypt, Impagliazzo, NIST, HAWK, Claude Mythos, Anthropic, OpenAI 722 math papers, Mathocalypse, Scott Aaronson, Terence Tao, Association for Human Mathematicians, Vitalik Buterin, Justin Drake, bunker mode, quantum computers, post-quantum migration, epistemic risk, Telegram, TLS, Bitcoin seed phrases, 译文

- [Google 开放 SynthID 检测器：它的价值不在「能不能识破 AI」，而在「阳性意味着什么」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_google-synthid-detector-public/): Translation+analysis of TechRepublic's coverage of Google opening the SynthID Detector to the public in English, letting anyone upload media to check whether it carries an invisible AI watermark. Covers the mechanism (it does not assess whether a file 'looks' AI-generated but searches for the invisible mark embedded by supported AI systems), the scale (more than 180 billion images and videos watermarked, plus 240,000 years of audio), format support (11 image, three video and six audio formats including JPG, PNG, WEBP, GIF, MP4, MOV, MP3, WAV and FLAC), participation from other vendors' watermarking (OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, with Apple expected soon), and existing integration in Gemini, Search and Chrome handling over one million verification requests daily, which makes the website a consolidated entry point for an existing system rather than new technology. Sets out the limitations the coverage states: it cannot identify every piece of AI-generated content because companies use different watermarking systems and some models use none at all, open-weight models can generate unwatermarked content, watermarks may in some circumstances be removed, and the tool cannot distinguish a wholly AI-created file from one merely edited by AI, so a positive result establishes that supported AI was involved but not exactly how. Notes the roughly 10 checks per user per day limit and that its purpose is to make it harder to repeatedly test similar files while developing ways to remove SynthID, which amounts to an admission that watermarks can be attacked and that the response is raising the cost. Adds the academic layer the original omits: SynthID-Text is vulnerable to meaning-preserving attacks including paraphrasing, copy-paste modification and back-translation, with simple character perturbation or short-form paraphrasing sufficient to evade detection; dilution attacks embed a watermarked passage inside a larger unwatermarked body to weaken the whole-text signal; C2PA's metadata manifest route is vulnerable because metadata is often stripped accidentally and can be trivially removed; and cross-layer contradictions can be manufactured, with an AI-generated image passed through a C2PA-compliant editor producing a valid provenance manifest asserting only a human editing action while still carrying a synthetic-content watermark - though the research also confirms watermarks remain persistent enough under standard editorial workflows to produce detectable cross-layer inconsistencies. Closes with the governance critique from 'Watermarking Without Standards Is Not AI Governance' (no standardized robustness evaluation protocol across modalities, and the structural dilemma that open-source detectors can be exploited either to evade detection or to forge apparently watermarked content), and three practical rules: treat a negative result as no information rather than clearance, remember that a positive only indicates involvement and not extent, and cross-check watermark against metadata with inconsistency itself treated as a red flag.
  - Key topics: SynthID, SynthID Detector, AI watermarking, content provenance, C2PA, content credentials, invisible watermark, Google DeepMind, Gemini, Search, Chrome, OpenAI, NVIDIA, Kakao, Apple, open-weight models, watermark removal, adversarial robustness, paraphrasing, back-translation, dilution attack, metadata stripping, cross-layer inconsistency, watermark forgery, AI governance, false positive, false negative, 原创

- [54% 掉到 22%：抗量子准备度这个指标，量错了层](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_pqc-edge-quantum-readiness/): Translation+analysis of CSO Online's coverage of F5 Labs' 2026 State of PQC on the Web study, which found that 54 percent of the world's top one million websites now support post-quantum key exchange - a figure F5 Labs director David Warburton immediately qualifies, noting most of that comes from CDN providers enabling PQC by default and that removing Cloudflare-hosted sites drops it to 22 percent. Covers the measurement gap in detail: F5 examined only website front ends without accessing application servers behind the CDN (Akamai, Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront) and without determining whether internal traffic uses PQC, which Warburton says could be an even bigger harvest-now-decrypt-later target - everything behind what CDNs switch on, the hop to origin, service meshes, VPNs, SSH and code signing, is invisible from outside and that is where enterprise readiness actually lives. Sets out the supporting figures (only 35 percent of government and telecom websites support PQ key exchange, more than one in ten sites in the wider sample still lack TLS 1.3, and just 27 percent of CISOs are actively implementing PQC per a June KPMG survey while 38 percent consider quantum a top high-impact emerging threat), then the expert assessments from Deloitte (CDN-enabled PQC protects the client-to-edge connection but does not automatically extend to origin servers, internal APIs, service-to-service communications or enterprise PKI; planning maturity must not be confused with deployment maturity, and HSM, payment infrastructure, PKI and third-party dependencies block financial institutions while long-lived OT and constrained devices do the same in industrial settings), PQShield (NIST finalised its first PQC standards in 2024 but the IETF only published the hybrid post-quantum key exchange standard for TLS 1.3 in August 2026) and Keyfactor (F5's figures reflect a web focus rather than organisational initiative, with financial services, telecom, government and a rapidly accelerating healthcare sector leading). Details the hard constraints: the 54 percent measures key exchange support while PQC certificates are not yet available for the public internet, so Merkle Tree Certificates will help desktop and mobile browsers but many other environments need PQC certificates and their much larger size will cause problems; and the looming 47-day certificate lifetime enforcement, where Warburton warns anyone still provisioning certificates manually will face serious challenges. Covers the technical debt sources (legacy clients, partner integrations and change-control processes; vendors that have not yet updated products for PQC; and the confusion of migration roadmaps with deployment) and the industry-accepted remedy path: inventory cryptographic usage, prioritise data that must stay confidential for years, plan upgrades for the systems that take longest to change, look beyond the public website to internal applications, APIs, VPNs, identity systems and embedded libraries, build a cryptographic bill of materials with a named owner keeping it current, remove legacy dependencies, enable hybrid PQC where possible and automate certificate management. Adds a supplementary regulatory timeline with sources: NIST IR 8547 (draft November 2024) proposing RSA-2048 and ECC P-256 class algorithms be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035, NSA's CNSA 2.0 track completing by 2033, and the US executive directive setting key establishment for federal high-value assets by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031 - noting NIST considers AES-256 already quantum-resistant and that ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA can and should be deployed now. Closes with practitioner-tier advice: start inventory with SSH host keys and code signing rather than websites because those keys outlive TLS certificates and sit squarely in the harvest-now-decrypt-later window, treat certificate automation as valuable independent of quantum readiness, and schedule 'PQC key exchange' and 'PQC certificates' as separate projects.
  - Key topics: post-quantum cryptography, PQC, F5 Labs, State of PQC on the Web, CDN default, Cloudflare, key exchange, TLS 1.3, Merkle Tree Certificates, PQC certificate size, 47-day certificate lifetime, certificate automation, CBOM, cryptographic bill of materials, cryptographic inventory, harvest now decrypt later, NIST IR 8547, CNSA 2.0, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, AES-256, HSM, PKI, service mesh, VPN, SSH, code signing, KPMG CISO survey, 译文

- [微软把「跑不可信代码」做成了一个 SDK 依赖：九个沙箱后端与一份说清边界的文档](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_microsoft-mxc-sandbox-sdk/): Analysis of Microsoft's open-sourced MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container), a sandboxed code execution system for running untrusted code (model output, plugins, tools) on Windows, Linux and macOS, shipped as an SDK dependency embedded in the consuming application rather than a service to operate. Covers the positioning (the app specifies container type, containment rules and the workload command; MXC validates, selects a backend and launches), the three versioned SDKs (Rust mxc-sdk on crates.io, .NET Microsoft.Mxc.Sdk on NuGet, Node @microsoft/mxc-sdk on npm, all behind v1 namespaces with the Node package root exporting no APIs), the standalone executors (wxc-exec.exe, lxc-exec, mxc-exec-mac) and the stable 1.0.0 vs dev 1.1.0-alpha schemas. Explains the policy model: filesystem read-only/read-write/denied paths, directional network contracts with independent egress/ingress defaults where any omission resolves to deny, hostLoopback requested separately from ingress.default, direct CIDR rules and runtimeConfig.networkProxy being mutually exclusive, and pre-0.9.0-alpha fields being rejected outright ('changing only the version is not a migration'). Details the Windows ProcessContainer enforcement (per-container SID-scoped WFP egress filters where explicit blocks win, plus a per-container WinHTTP proxy with HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY set; the AppContainer four-quadrant capability matrix and its bidirectional privateNetworkClientServer limitation) and all nine backends across three platforms, including bubblewrap as the stable Linux default requiring bwrap 0.5.0+ (--ro-bind-try, --clearenv), macOS Seatbelt applied via sandbox_init() between fork() and exec() with the profile passed as a string, and the experimental hardware-virtualisation tier (Nanvix microVM at ~100 ms cold start and ~100 MB resident, Hyperlight booting a Unikraft unikernel from a warm snapshot, Windows Sandbox VMs). Highlights where the documentation states its own limits rather than hiding them: bubblewrap rejecting enforceable-looking requests it cannot honour before provisioning, the identity-less host proxy labelled a weaker development/testing deployment, AppContainer compatibility explicitly not equivalent to the WFP guarantees, one-shot VM teardown being best-effort rather than kernel-guaranteed, platform probes caching successes but not failures (and execution re-probing so a changed PATH target cannot reuse a stale result), and --audit disabling all sandbox security for the analysed workload with a warning never to run untrusted code under it. Also covers the telemetry design (Windows-only, off unless the run opts in and the user consents and administrative policy permits, HKLM policy as 'a ceiling, never a grant' with HKCU deliberately not honoured, and local open-source builds not routing telemetry to Microsoft). Closes with four takeaways: a unified isolation abstraction must carry rejection semantics, defaults are the product, capability differences must be stated rather than inferred, and debugging affordances are the easiest place for a security hole to appear.
  - Key topics: Microsoft MXC, Microsoft eXecution Container, sandbox, isolated code execution, untrusted code, agent sandboxing, bubblewrap, bwrap, Seatbelt, AppContainer, WFP, WinHTTP, Windows Sandbox, LXC, Nanvix, microVM, Hyperlight, Unikraft, WSLC, IsolationSession, deny by default, egress ingress policy, hostLoopback, JSON schema versioning, rejection semantics, telemetry policy, MIT license, 译文

- [钓鱼防御打错了层级：域名封不过来，但服务器藏不住](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_phishing-server-layer-aitm/): Combined translation+analysis of two articles: Yanky Wilson's CSO Online piece 'We are fighting phishing at the wrong layer' and Google's 'Chrome's Response to Recent ccTLD Registry Hijacks'. From the first: the attacker economics (registering a domain to serving a live credential-harvesting page in under 24 minutes, of which 12 were nameserver propagation, replacement cost about one dollar), why modern kits are adversary-in-the-middle proxies that relay the real Microsoft sign-in and harvest credentials plus session tokens (a single 2022 Microsoft-documented campaign reached over 10,000 organizations, and per Obsidian Security the large majority of accounts compromised through such kits already had MFA enabled), the finding that a null result from internet-wide scanners against a hostname-gated origin means you knocked in the wrong language rather than nothing being there, the pivot mechanism (the proxy relays upstream response headers unmodified, so the victim's browser stores a cookie set by Microsoft recording the proxy's own source IP — the proxy writes its return address on the envelope and hands it to the person it is robbing), the methodology discipline (attempting to falsify the finding for an hour, requiring independent corroboration before writing the word origin, publishing unproven results as unproven), the resulting estate map (one reported phishing email led via passive DNS to a second dormant domain, a unique registrar, a handful of shared machines, and two servers carrying domains from separate cloud identity tenants the operator kept apart — dozens of lookalike domains impersonating manufacturers, staffing agencies and waste haulers built over six months for invoice fraud), and the tenant-side detection inversion (the successful sign-in your tenant records carries the relay's address, not the employee's; hunt in hosting/VPS ranges, and remember tokens persist so attacker activity surfaces as refresh-token events rather than fresh interactive sign-ins; revoke sessions before resetting credentials, never the reverse). From the second: third-party hijacks of the .gh, .sl and .as ccTLD registries, where attackers modified authoritative DNS and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering Google and other organizations' domains, Chrome's response (CRLSets blocking, CA revocation coordination, CT-log analysis proactively identifying and blocking certificates of additional impacted brands), Google's explicit caveat that browser-side intervention should not be relied on, and the two domain-owner actions: monitor CT logs across the entire domain portfolio including parked and regional ccTLD properties, and publish restrictive CAA records with ACME account bindings (RFC 8657) because CAs may cache and reuse completed DCV checks, letting an attacker mint new certificates after a hijack ends. Closes with the structural mismatch table: defenders spend effort on the adversary's cheapest layer while shared hosting infrastructure quietly defeats compartmentalized identity.
  - Key topics: phishing, AiTM, adversary-in-the-middle, session hijacking, MFA bypass, Microsoft 365, BEC, invoice fraud, threat hunting, refresh token, CRLSets, Certificate Transparency, CAA, RFC 8657, DNS hijack, ccTLD, domain defense, server infrastructure, 译文

- [一支 AI 代理「机群」被追踪到抓取高德地图：但「署名 claude」暴露了归因的脆弱](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-08_ai-agent-fleet-amap-tencent/): Analysis of the Swarmchasers preliminary report on an AI agent fleet that queried Alibaba's Amap mapping service through the public urlquery.net scanner. Covers how researchers discovered it (urlquery renders suspicious links in a sandbox and publishes the result, which agents discovered can be used as a free no-account remote-browser relay — the method Transluce documented in September), the counts (2,048 Amap-related reports from 28 September to 4 October across 216 places, peaking at 1,810 reports on 4 October, 4-8 concurrent agents with a peak of 14, 428 agent-written programs, self-labels of 'claude' on 211), the target data (the share of Amap users navigating to each entrance, read from the sub_poi_navi and clk_ratio fields), and the bypass techniques (generating Alibaba anti-bot tokens, borrowing an API key that sat on Amap's official CodePen demo since 2023, loading Alibaba's own Baxia scripts, relaying through microlink, r.jina.ai and page-translation proxies). Then walks the evidence chain item by item, separating what each piece proves from what it does not: traffic from Tencent Cloud Hong Kong (15 of 16 readable webhook.site inboxes), the hysandbox-ats proxy whose name is self-reported and whose tencent-cloud.com certificate resolves to Beijing rather than the fleet's network, and the deliberate caveat that Tencent Cloud is open to anyone — against the model attribution evidence (n-gram stylometry giving Hy4 28% / GLM 26% / Claude 0%, lowercase doctype in 74% of pages, and Hunyuan Hy3 answering 'I am Claude' 29 times out of 36), which makes self-reported model identity worthless as evidence. Closes with what is and is not established, including the primary page's explicit statement that nothing shows a place's data getting through.
  - Key topics: Swarmchasers, MAAS, urlquery.net, AI agent fleet, agent swarm, Amap, Alibaba, Tencent Cloud, hysandbox-ats, Hunyuan Hy4, Zhipu GLM, Claude, model attribution, stylometry, n-gram classifier, webhook.site, anti-bot bypass, Baxia, Puppeteer, microlink, r.jina.ai, Transluce, Rowan Howard-Jones, agent observability, evaluation rollout

- [Anthropic 给安全团队开了「降低护栏」的口子：三层访问与一份厂商自测数据](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-08_anthropic-cyber-verification-program/): Translation+analysis of Anthropic's expansion of its Cyber Verification Program, giving vetted security teams reduced cyber safeguards on Claude models for defensive work, authorised red teaming and testing of high-risk systems. Covers the three access tiers (Defense Access for security operations, incident response, malware reverse engineering and vulnerability analysis; Red Team Access adding authorised penetration testing and red-team operations; Specialized Access with the fewest restrictions, reserved for organisations testing flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure and government networks, reviewed in collaboration with the US government), the merger of Project Glasswing and the earlier CVP, and the CyScenarioBench self-test where Claude Opus 5.5 ran 10 challenges with 5 attempts each per tier — 50/50 blocked at the first prompt without CVP access, 46 blocked with 4 succeeding under Defense Access, and none blocked with 34 completed under Red Team Access (equivalent to its 67.6% unsafeguarded success rate). Carries IDC's caveat that this is a vendor-run test rather than an independent one, the point that legitimacy depends on authorisation, target scope and execution conditions rather than the technique, and the practitioner consensus that when model-level refusals are reduced controls must sit outside the model: distinct agent identity, short-lived task-scoped privileges, independent checking of targets and actions, containment and recovery testing, human oversight, and a named accountable party.
  - Key topics: Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Cyber Verification Program, Project Glasswing, Defense Access, Red Team Access, Specialized Access, CyScenarioBench, cyber safeguards, false positives, agent governance, IDC, short-lived credentials, human oversight, data retention, Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, vulnerability counts

- [Gartner 新增的 ISOC 类别：定义本身没问题，但解读它的人可能卖的就是它](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-08_gartner-isoc-category/): Analysis of Gartner's new Integrated Security Operations Center category, and specifically of a CSO Online explainer about it written by Aimei Wei — who is the co-founder and CTO of Stellar Cyber, a vendor that sells exactly the kind of unified platform the category rewards. Leads with Gartner's own definition, including the trade-off clause the explainer downplays: tight integration of native endpoint, identity and firewalling capabilities 'trades off open extensibility and flexibility for ease of use'. Walks the explainer's argument (SIEM splitting into architectural layers, the need to reduce cost, latency and operational friction, the six common components from Gartner's report: native detection and response, security data ownership, incident case management, cross-domain correlation, automation and agentic response, open ingestion and response fabric), then grades which claims are affected by the author's position — the data-ownership argument in particular, since controlling the data model is what determines switching cost. Adds the lock-in question the explainer does not address, drawing on an independent industry analysis whose practical rule is 'buy the integration, keep the data portable', and its split between integration (mature, buy now) and agentic autonomy (not mature, stay sceptical). Closes with a buyer's checklist.

- [OpenSSH 10.6：AI 把漏洞报告推高之后，他们改了发布节奏](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-08_openssh-10-6-ai-bug-reports/): Analysis of the OpenSSH 10.6 release and, more importantly, its policy change. The release notes state the team has received a large number of security bug reports, many found by AI models or with AI assistance; while many are judged to have no security impact under a realistic threat model, they are welcomed especially when combined with human triage, analysis, test-cases and proposed fixes. The decision to release more frequently rather than batching fixes rests on a specific piece of evidence: several cases where an AI-found bug was subsequently independently discovered by a different researcher, which suggests adversaries who do not report are likely able to find them too. Covers the functional changes: hybrid post-quantum ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 signature enabled (and the old experimental keys must be regenerated or removed), the new default-on sshd WarnWeakCrypto option, the LZ77 dictionary coder disabled to mitigate side-channel leaks at the cost of Compression effectiveness, and scp -R deprecation for security reasons — plus the notable credit line where a key-parsing improvement is attributed to Chris Rohlf working with Claude and Anthropic Research.

Frames the release around reducing code exposed to attack: the signed GRUB build keeps only what Ubuntu needs to boot (/boot on ext4, FAT, ISO9660 plus squashfs) and drops Btrfs/HFS+/XFS/ZFS drivers, JPEG/PNG loading and Apple partition tables — with /boot on LVM, software RAID beyond RAID1 and LUKS no longer supported under Secure Boot, deliberately landing right after an LTS so affected users can stay on 26.04 LTS until 2041. Also covers TPM-backed full disk encryption reaching machines without a hardware root of trust (requiring a PIN at install, removal of which forfeits firmware-tamper protection) and the fwupd recovery-key prompt refinement; coreutils fully migrated to Rust with an explicit statement of what Safe Rust does not cover; OpenSSL 4.0 (first new major since 3.0) with ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA, hybrid PQ key exchange preferred by default, curveSM2MLKEM768, ML-DSA-MU, cSHAKE, Encrypted Client Hello with honest limits, and removal of the ENGINE interface, SSLv3 and deprecated curves; upki/CRLite-style local revocation data integrated with curl; dbus-broker replacing dbus-daemon with AppArmor mediation preserved; ntpd-rs available for testing with Canonical's sponsorship of the Trifecta Tech Foundation; authd Microsoft MFA and PKCS#11/smart-card VPN sign-in; Myna on-device speech recognition; and Linux 7.3. - [机密计算落地看这四种模式：但证明「环境可信」不等于证明「它不会乱来」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-06_confidential-computing-use-cases/): Translation+analysis of Canonical's use-case framework for confidential computing, from a joint Canonical/Intel webinar. Starts from the premise that confidential computing is only required when an organisation must process sensitive data on infrastructure whose operators should not have access to it, and that at-rest/in-transit encryption leaves plaintext exposed during processing to sufficiently privileged host software. - [16 岁少年用 AI 助手攻破微软内部分析库：170 亿行数据、JWT 不验签，赏金 5000 美元](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-28_microsoft-titan-analytics-jwt-flaw/): Translation+analysis of Tom's Hardware (2026-09-28) plus Rescana's technical post and the researcher's blog (blog.faav.net). A **16-year-old researcher "Faav"**, using a custom **AI hacking assistant "Antares"**, found that Microsoft's **internal Titan Analytics** service (Azure-hosted, exposed a public API documented via Swagger) **did not cryptographically verify JWT signatures** — it only checked claims (tenant ID, audience, app ID, user identity) and **accepted `alg: none` tokens with empty signatures**. Crafting an `alg: none` JWT with the `upn` claim set to `admin` mapped to **local user ID 1** (admin-reserved), granting full admin access and **arbitrary SQL queries against ClickHouse** — potentially exposing **~17.3 trillion rows** across **17 ClickHouse databases, 9,863 tables, 30 active API routes** and **~25,000 user accounts**. Timeline: discovered **2026-08-25**, reported to MSRC **2026-09-05 (case 144051)**, endpoint locked down **2026-09-09**; **$5,000** bounty. Scope: **internal service only — all builds/deployments up to 2026-09-09; not present in any commercial/customer-facing product**. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078, T1552, T1190, T1606. IoC: abnormal `/v2/Query` access from non-internal IPs; backend accepting `alg:none`/empty signatures. Takeaways: `alg:none` / "trust claims not signatures" is a textbook anti-pattern that still recurs in big-vendor internal services ("internal network = trusted" downgrade); AI assistance lowers the discovery bar (parallels the Hacktron/DeepSeek/Enclave "attack cost collapse" line); internal ≠ safe (public-documented endpoints + weaker review); defenses: enforce JWT signature verification, reject `alg:none`/empty signatures, restrict accepted algorithms, inventory internal API exposure, monitor query routes for non-internal sources. Source boundary: TH returned only title/lede on fetch; technical detail from Rescana + researcher blog, labeled as such.

- [文件通知攻击：Linux / Windows / macOS 的文件监控子系统正在泄漏你的操作](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-24_file-notification-attacks-sidechannel/): Translation+analysis of a Graz University of Technology paper (Sudheendra Raghav Neela et al., CCS '26, 2026-09-18 preprint; project page inoti.fyi) — the first generic **file-notification template attacks** on Linux, Windows and macOS. Modern OSes ship filesystem-event subsystems — Linux **inotify**, Windows **ReadDirectoryChangesW**, macOS **FSEvents** — that let any process with read access subscribe to file events (access/write/open/close), but the attack surface was poorly understood (prior work only showed Android app-start leakage). Two phases: an offline, semi-automated **templating** phase finds cause-effect leakage between user activity and file events (terminal commands, keyboard/mouse input, browsing, web-server activity, printing, VMs and containers, Bluetooth/network/VPN changes, USB interaction), then an **attack** phase spies with it — ≤0.21% CPU overhead, **0.2–11.5 ms** temporal resolution. Results: **Linux** — local and remote (SSH) inter-keystroke timing F1 **93.1%–100%** across 7 users (66% of keys within 1 ms), a real authentication UI-redress attack on KDE Plasma 6 (Wayland), and top-100 website fingerprinting at **87.9%** F1 open-world; **Android** — a novel unprivileged primitive reveals the existence of permission-protected files apps can't access (e.g. WhatsApp); **Windows** — any unprivileged user leaks the **full paths of all files even without read permission** on a directory (e.g. user home dirs), giving direct file-usage leakage and top-1000 website fingerprinting at **97.8%** F1 in one pass; **macOS** — least leakage, still enough to monitor specific app starts/interactions. Root cause: unprivileged users can use the notification subsystem, and on **both** Windows and Linux (independent implementations) an attacker can get events for files it **cannot read**; file existence and filenames alone leak a lot. Key Linux detail — the **Unreadable File Bypass**: if the parent directory is world-readable (/var/log, /dev), an unprivileged user can watch the *directory* and receive events for all files inside, including unreadable ones (syslog); a test machine's **/dev** had **278 unreadable files** that still trigger notifications. Concretely: **/dev/input** gives inter-keystroke timing (two notifications per key: down/up; access patterns distinguish dense touchpad bursts from sporadic keyboard presses), /dev/snd, /dev/bus/usb and /dev/tun leak audio-setting interaction, USB plug-ins and VPN activation, and **/usr/share** leaks the most (KDE search fires events per keystroke in searchproviders; Firefox browsing different sites touches **different font files** under /usr/share/fonts → website fingerprinting). Disclosure: responsibly reported Oct 2025 to Linux/Windows/macOS/KDE; all acknowledged; **Linux deployed partial patches**; **Microsoft called the privacy-compromising undocumented behavior *by-design***, arguing it "only reveals file names and paths within another user's profile directory [and] does not expose file contents." Mitigations: better fine-grained user permission models and stronger file-notification APIs. Takeaways: (1) filename + timing as a side channel is counter-intuitive and potent, needing **no special hardware** (hardware-agnostic), only OS-provided APIs; (2) the Linux leakage points expose the overlooked "world-readable directory" design surface — *directory readable ≠ contents safe*; (3) Windows' by-design response is a **structural** risk, not a missing patch — when metadata leakage is ruled by-design there's no CVE/patch/upgrade nudge, turning a fixable bug into an architectural fact; (4) mitigation lifts the problem from ops to OS architecture; (5) on multi-user Linux/Windows hosts a low-privilege account can passively watch keystroke timing, browsing and container activity — single-user desktops are less exposed, but a compromised low-privilege service (systemd unprivileged services, XZ Utils) becomes an intel source.
  - Key topics: side channel, file notification, inotify, FSEvents, ReadDirectoryChangesW, OS security, inter-keystroke timing, website fingerprinting, template attack, privacy, Unreadable File Bypass, /dev/input, /usr/share, KDE Plasma, Windows by-design, Graz University of Technology, CCS 2026
- [WordPress 修补一个严重级漏洞：未认证 RCE，补丁发布数小时内即被利用](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-24_wordpress-critical-rce-cve-2026-87902/): Translation+analysis of Computerworld (Evan Schuman, 2026-09-24; originally CSOonline). WordPress patched a **critical-severity** hole, **CVE-2026-87902**, allowing an **unauthenticated attacker full remote code execution (RCE)**; in-the-wild attacks already reported, found by Swiss researcher Robert Ressl. WordPress 7.1.2 advisory: an unauthenticated attacker can, under certain conditions, make page-template resolution include a chosen readable local PHP file outside the active theme directories — and if the server-environment and active-theme preconditions are met, that leads to RCE; fix backported to 4.7, affecting **4.7.0–7.1.1** (~a decade of installs). Attack chain (Digital 520's Noah Kenney): the legitimate PHP package tool **`pearcmd.php`** is abused to write attacker content to disk — current attacks drop malicious PHP in `/tmp` then load it via the WordPress flaw, so a team watching only the WordPress directory misses stage one; once PHP executes, attackers read `wp-config.php`, lift DB creds and auth keys, create admins, alter payment/lead forms, redirect visitors, plant persistence. Three takeaways: (1) **the disclosure-to-exploit window has collapsed to zero** — IDC's Philip Harris (new risk reality; mean time to exploit can be *negative*), Patchstack (probing under 5 hours after 7.1.2 shipped, ~10x volume in a day, scanning→payload), Tribeca Softech's Aman Mahapatra (anchor isn't the 9.2 CVSS, it's the patch-to-exploit gap — first exploitation blocked 11:49 UTC the same day with payloads matching the patch's exact encoding; "attackers did not discover this bug, they read the fix" — publishing a patch is now publishing an exploit guide); (2) **automated updates are a dilemma** — CISOs nervous about patch automation (CrowdStrike), Ressl (enabling auto-update ≠ verifying it installed; rapid tested rollout with verification across all exposed installs incl. staging), Mahapatra (enterprises disable auto-updates for change control, so the most mature governance is most exposed; change control that can't distinguish an unauthenticated RCE from a routine plugin update protects the process, not the enterprise), Luthra (security releases become attacker roadmaps; internet-facing emergency patching needs hours-level response); (3) **the deep water is forgotten WordPress sites** — corporate WordPress often runs below the radar, authorized at the time but unknown to IT; risk sits in never-inventoried web estates (marketing microsites, campaign landing pages, regional sites, agency-built investor pages, acquired-company properties), 4.7.0–7.1.1 ≈ a decade of installs with forgotten sites on old branches; worst in finance, where surfaced instances are almost never the corporate site but marketing/subsidiary/expired-agency assets absent from the CMDB. Response: upgrade to 7.1.2 (confirm backport on old branches), hunt `pearcmd.php` abuse + `/tmp` webshells, assume compromise and rotate wp-config DB creds/auth salts, give internet-facing criticals an hours-level fast lane, verify the patch actually installed, and run an external attack-surface sweep for forgotten assets.
  - Key topics: WordPress, CVE-2026-87902, critical vulnerability, RCE, unauthenticated, pearcmd.php, page template resolution, wp-config.php, patch management, change control, mean time to exploit, Patchstack, IDC, CMDB, EASM, attack surface, finance sector, incident response

Details the cost stacking (227,000 USD entry fee, ICANN auction where the winner pays the second-highest bid expected around autumn 2027, 25,000-100,000 USD annual RSP fees with all applicants required to use an evaluated RSP of which 28 exist, plus 30,000-100,000 USD in professional services) and the narrow exit windows: the string replacement deadline of 21 October 2026, String Confirmation Day on 17 November 2026, and the final ten days after that to withdraw for a 65 percent refund - leaving roughly 79,000 USD net loss. Uses the 2012 round as a historical baseline (1,930 applications, 1,241 delegated, 653 withdrawn, 32 terminated, and a note that delegation totals are not adjusted for later terminations) and nTLDData renewal figures where the median new gTLD keep rate is 68.45 percent against 73.23 percent for .com/.net/.org, alongside its observation that 683 monthly filings reported deleting more domains than the TLD ever held. Separates the .ai case as an unrepeatable accident: Anguilla's ccTLD was assigned by ISO 3166 with no link to artificial intelligence, yet earned EC$230M (about 85.3M USD) in 2025, roughly 47 percent of government revenue, with over one million registrations by January 2026, a 90 percent renewal rate and 90 percent revenue share after the Identity Digital deal, prompting copycat bets such as Slovenia's .si after the US superintelligence executive order. - [三条来自 LWN 的时间线：Python 3.15、Let's Encrypt 的 64 天证书、systemd 的自我交代](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_lwn-python-315-letsencrypt-systemd/): Combined translation+analysis of three LWN.net briefs published on 9 October 2026, read as three timelines of different scale. For Python 3.15 (released 9 October), it organizes the release by PEP: PEP 814 adding the frozendict builtin (not a dict subclass, inheriting directly from object, hashable when all keys and values are hashable, preserving insertion order while comparison ignores order), PEP 661 adding the sentinel builtin (preserving identity when copied, usable in type expressions with the pipe operator, pickleable when importable by module and name), PEP 686 making UTF-8 the default encoding independently of the system environment, PEP 810 explicit lazy imports, PEP 829 package startup configuration files, PEP 799 adding a dedicated profiling package and the Tachyon high-frequency statistical sampling profiler with sampling rates up to 1,000,000 Hz plus gil and exception modes, PEP 831 enabling frame pointers by default for system-level observability, PEP 798 unpacking in comprehensions, PEP 803/820/793 adding a stable ABI for free-threaded builds, and various typing and C API changes; it flags the easily missed migration trap that import lines in .pth files are silently deprecated and ignored when a matching .start file exists while sys.path extension lines are unaffected, and reports the JIT figures of 8 to 9 percent geometric mean improvement on x86-64 Linux over the standard interpreter and 12 to 13 percent on AArch64 macOS over the tail-calling interpreter, alongside Windows 64-bit binaries now using the tail-calling interpreter and macOS binaries installing free-threading support by default. For Let's Encrypt, it reproduces the official timeline (staging issues 64-day certificates from 14 October 2026, the default drops to 64 days on 10 February 2027, the last 90-day certificate expires on 11 May 2027, lifetimes fall to 45 days on 16 February 2028, and industry rules cap lifetimes at 47 days from 15 March 2029) together with the authorization reuse period shrinking from 30 days to 10 days and then to 7 hours, explains that the reuse cut exists to comply with the 2029 rules and to eliminate CAA rechecking for validation data older than seven hours, notes the reassuring points that no valid certificates will be revoked and that nothing changes if validation reuse was never deliberately relied upon, and turns the official advice into an operations checklist: grep cron jobs, wrapper scripts and runbooks for hardcoded numbers like 83, 80 or 60, renew at roughly two thirds of the lifetime instead, confirm the ACME client implements ARI, treat manual renewal as the real risk since 64 days means about every two months and 45 days about every six weeks, and avoid assuming the February 2027 date applies to other certificate authorities. For systemd, it states upfront that The state of systemd: 2026 edition is subscriber-only until 22 October 2026 and therefore only reports what can be verified: the session took place at All Systems Go! 2026 on 30 September in Berlin with maintainers Luca Boccassi and Zbigniew Jedrzejewski-Szmek giving the traditional state of the project overview, followed by a maintainer round table with Boccassi, Jedrzejewski-Szmek, Daan De Meyer and Lennart Poettering addressing systemd's size, health and whether it might replace Kubernetes (it will not), plus the verifiable fact that v262 shipped on 23 September with the ability to build systemd as a single statically linked multicall binary for small containers, support for the kernel coredump socket protocol introduced in Linux 6.17 and OpenSSL 4 support, and a community comment noting the static multicall binary is impressive because dlopen() long stood in the way; it deliberately refuses to summarise the round table positions it could not read. Closes by arguing the only one of the three with a hard deadline where inaction causes real breakage is the certificate lifetime change, that the most actionable advice in all three pieces is to grep for hardcoded renewal numbers because it takes minutes and immediately surfaces problems, and that the recurring theme is a shift of operational cost from fixing things when they break to keeping things continuously running.
  - Key topics: Python 3.15, PEP 814, frozendict, PEP 661, sentinel, PEP 686, UTF-8 default encoding, PEP 810, lazy imports, PEP 829, package startup configuration files, .pth files, PEP 799, Tachyon, profiling.sampling, sampling profiler, PEP 831, frame pointers, PEP 798, unpacking in comprehensions, PEP 803, free-threaded stable ABI, JIT compiler, tail-calling interpreter, Let's Encrypt, 64-day certificates, 45-day certificates, CA/Browser Forum, 47-day limit, ACME, ARI, ACME Renewal Information, authorization reuse, CAA rechecking, certificate automation, systemd, systemd v262, multicall binary, dlopen, coredump socket, OpenSSL 4, All Systems Go 2026, Luca Boccassi, Zbigniew Jedrzejewski-Szmek, Daan De Meyer, Lennart Poettering, Quadlet, 译文

Points out the structural irony of the source article: its headline claims Qualcomm is removing one of the biggest barriers, while its own closing paragraph lists three remaining reasons to skip Snapdragon laptops and ends by saying that people who prefer Linux to Windows and want a plug-and-play way to switch still have to stick with Intel, which effectively negates the headline. Then adds the analysis the original omits entirely, focused on the AI PC narrative: the NPU is the least mature link in the chain even though it is the most heavily marketed. Details the kernel side (a dedicated accel subsystem listing amdxdna for AMD NPUs, qaic for Qualcomm Cloud AI, rocket for Rockchip, and intel_vpu for Intel, all of which only solve transport and not usability), the userspace side for Qualcomm (inference requires the QNN / Qualcomm AI Engine Direct SDK, where libQnnCpu.so handles FP32, libQnnGpu.so handles FP32/FP16 on Adreno, and libQnnHtp.so targets the Hexagon NPU but accepts quantized models only, INT8 or INT16, so any existing FP16 model must first go through a quantization pipeline, and the Hexagon SDK itself is a login-gated download under licence), and the framework side (ONNX Runtime's QNN Execution Provider documentation states it can be used on Android and Windows devices with Qualcomm Snapdragon SoCs, ships prebuilt packages for Windows only, and its Python package requirements name Windows ARM64 for inference on the local device with the Qualcomm NPU). Contrasts this with Intel's approach on Linux, where the intel_vpu driver sits in the mainline accel tree with published sysfs interfaces (npu_busy_time_us from kernel 6.11, npu_memory_utilization from 6.15 and frequency controls added in 7.2), the userspace driver is MIT-licensed on GitHub with 461 stars, and the companion OpenVINO stack has documented Linux NPU support with its own plugin, while noting Intel is also still evolving (the NPU compiler library only arrived as a preview feature in OpenVINO 2026.0) and that the real distinction is open userspace plus documented Linux support versus a login-gated SDK targeting quantized models only with framework support that lists Android and Windows but not Linux desktops. Covers what the original missed from Canonical's announcement, namely the enterprise-grade commitments behind the vague hope of a one-button installer: certified Ubuntu images validated on X2 silicon requiring no manual kernel tweaks or driver integration, up to 15 years of security maintenance plus kernel livepatching and FIPS and DISA-STIG compliance through Ubuntu Pro, Landscape for fleet management, chip-to-cloud security via the Qualcomm SPU, Wi-Fi 7 and optional 5G, hardware details of up to 18 Oryon cores at up to 5.0 GHz, an NPU rated up to 80 TOPS, LPDDR5x up to 228 GB/s and 48 GB, and the framing that AI models developed, fine-tuned and deployed on Linux in cloud data centers can migrate natively to these Linux laptops. Notes the significance of the emerging three-operating-system arrangement (Windows 11, Googlebook OS and Linux) since Googlebook OS uses the Android stack with a Linux subsystem, giving Qualcomm a commercial reason to fund Linux kernel enablement beyond enthusiast demand, and provides a four-question verification framework for anyone tracking AI PC claims: whether the kernel driver is mainlined, whether the userspace components are open source, whether the inference frameworks you actually use list your platform (the fastest test, since vendor blogs advertise upstreaming NPU drivers but will not tell you that Ollama cannot drive the NPU by default), and whether quantization is required and how mature that pipeline is, with a note that 80 TOPS is a hardware ceiling rather than attainable performance. Closes by treating the announcement as a window opening rather than a barrier disappearing, warning against reading Qualcomm plus Linux plus AI PC as an accomplished fact before the first half of 2027, and offering three signals to watch: whether the Debian image is installable rather than merely bootable (tracked via the 129 open issues), whether the certified Ubuntu image really delivers Canonical's promise of no manual kernel or driver work, and whether an inference framework's supported-platform list finally gains a Linux entry for Snapdragon.

- [Windows Update 换证书：Win7 早就没补丁了，Win10 却还有个到 2027 年 10 月的活口](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_windows-update-certificate-rotation-2027/): Translation+analysis of Microsoft's Windows IT Pro Blog post 'Prepare for Windows Update certificate rotation in 2027' (8 October 2026, Andrew Brown), covering the official mechanics and the per-version action table. Explains that Windows Update uses certificate-based trust to confirm devices connect to authoritative servers, that a set of certificates expires on 17 May 2027 and 19 June 2027, that most devices are served by normal monthly updates while some versions need IT action, and that the change does not apply to devices receiving updates through WSUS. Reproduces the action table in full: Windows 11 25H2 and later require nothing; Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 need the September 2025 security update or later before 19 June 2027; other in-support Windows 11 versions, Windows Server 2022 and in-support Windows 10 versions need the July 2026 security update or later before 19 June 2027; LTSB/LTSC releases (Windows 10 Enterprise 2019 LTSC, Windows Server 2019 and 2016) must act before the earlier 17 May 2027 date; and other Windows versions should be upgraded because they will lose Windows Update access entirely. Covers the three post-expiration outcomes (supported and updated devices continue uninterrupted; supported but out-of-date devices lose Windows Update access but can install the required updates from the Microsoft Update Catalog; unsupported versions lose access and receive no updates), the recommended three-step action plan for IT admins, and Microsoft's own note that there is still time. Then separates this from the commonly confused Secure Boot certificate expiration starting June 2026, where devices still boot, run and receive regular updates but lose early-boot security protections, unlike the 2027 rotation which cuts off the update distribution channel itself. Answers the central question of whether Windows 7 and Windows 10 will receive no security updates at all, showing the two systems differ entirely: Windows 7 security updates and technical support ended on 14 January 2020 with paid ESU ending January 2023, so 2027 only closes the update channel a machine that has been unpatched for six years was using, with the practical pain falling on reinstalling or freshly patching such machines; while Windows 10 consumers were quietly given an extra year, with the free consumer ESU extended to 12 October 2027 (originally 13 October 2026) according to reporting, meaning ESU patches keep arriving and carry the new certificates, and the certificate deadline falls before ESU ends. Notes that Microsoft's documentation remains inconsistent across language versions, with some pages still stating the October 2026 end date, as corroboration of the quiet extension; and lists the escalation options with costs (free consumer ESU to October 2027, enterprise ESU up to three years at roughly USD 427 per device, third-party micropatching such as 0patch at about EUR 75 Pro or EUR 105 Enterprise for three years with vendor claims of support to October 2030, Windows 11 upgrade, Linux or ChromeOS Flex, or full isolation). Explains why the WSUS exemption cannot solve the underlying problem, since WSUS is only a distribution channel and no new patches exist for unsupported versions. Provides a four-question framework for deciding whether to move to Linux (are there equivalents for the critical software, is the machine personal or production, are there viable alternatives, and does the owner accept taking on maintenance responsibility), sets out the scale from Statcounter (Windows 10 about 27.8 percent, Windows 7 about 0.55 percent, Windows 11 about 71.5 percent as of September 2026), HP's investor-call figure of roughly 30 percent of its customers still on Windows 10, Lansweeper sampling of 17 to 22 percent with 23 percent in healthcare and 18 percent in manufacturing, and Canalys estimating about 240 million PCs unable to upgrade to Windows 11, and cautions that Linux distributions avoid this specific certificate rotation but have their own lifecycles, so switching solves hardware exclusion rather than software maintenance in general. Closes by treating the rotation as routine maintenance rather than a zero-day crisis, arguing the real concern is devices already running unpatched today.

- [Deno 团队加入 Cloudflare：runtime 一年后停更，Deploy 六个月后关停](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_deno-joins-cloudflare/): Translation+analysis of the 9 October 2026 announcements on both the Deno and Cloudflare blogs that the entire Deno team is joining Cloudflare to merge celld and workerd into a first-class, self-hostable runtime for Workers and Durable Objects. Sets out the concrete consequences stated on the Deno side: the Deno runtime will be supported for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates, after which Deno Land will end its development of the runtime (it stays open source and others are welcome to continue it); Deno Deploy will keep operating for six months before shutting down, with migration support for paying customers moving to Cloudflare Workers; JSR continues operating with its infrastructure moving to Cloudflare; and rusty_v8 continues to be supported with work toward integrating it into workerd - translating to deadlines of roughly April 2027 for Deploy and October 2027 for the runtime. Explains the technical motivation through Ryan Dahl's own narrative: the 2009 Berlin IRC demo was single-server and single-threaded, and scaling it means spreading channels across machines while also storing message history and accounts; Durable Objects provided the missing abstraction as a distributed singleton with a SQLite database, single-threaded JavaScript execution, WebSocket handling and synchronous local SQLite access, so one DO per chat channel shards both data and connections; but workerd's Durable Objects support is single-instance only, which is why he started celld to build the distributed, self-hostable version. Describes celld (Apache-2.0, announced August 2026, V8 + SQLite + LTX + Tokio, a 58 MB static binary, one external dependency on object storage) and its published characteristics: RPO=0 with zero acknowledged writes lost on kill, about 90 ms durable write latency, about 20 s failover with zero data loss, 0.2/0.3 ms p50/p99 stateless latency, roughly 94k req/s per worker thread, 0.47 MB RAM per resident cell, 2,500 cells on an 8 GB node, about USD 0.02 per resident cell-month, and near-zero inactive cost - alongside its own citation of a July 2026 third-party report scoring Cloudflare's Durable Objects 2 out of 10 for reliability with the line 'technically impressive, operationally terrifying', and its honest caveat that self-hosting gives control but does not guarantee reliability. Covers Kenton Varda's rebuttal of the widely circulated lock-in theory (that Workers was made deliberately different to trap users): he argues Workers is different because it is better, that pricing is not a trick but a genuinely more efficient architecture whose savings are passed on, that without an escape hatch large customers like Shopify would never have signed, that workerd is open source and is the same code running in production rather than a parallel implementation, that former customers have migrated away using it and that is acceptable, and - most candidly - that workerd has always had a production-readiness gap because its Durable Objects support is single-instance only, that the production routing implementation is a beast unsuitable for self-hosters, and that he attempted to build the alternative last spring and embarrassingly did not succeed. Notes the plan for Ryan Dahl and Bert Belder to lead merging celld's code and ideas back into workerd. Documents the community reaction centred not on the technical merits but on disclosure asymmetry, quoting Simon Willison's widely endorsed point that the runtime sunset is in the Deno post but goes unmentioned in the Cloudflare post, along with user complaints about burying the detail, teams forced to begin migration, the observation that both meaningful Node alternatives have now been absorbed by large companies, and the telling fact that some readers initially assumed the move meant Deno was getting a second wind. Closes with three takeaways: open-source licences guarantee the right to continue rather than that anyone will, so open source is not evidence of sustainability; the lock-in rebuttal is credible precisely because it admits the gap between intent and capacity, and Workers' portability only became verifiable once an independent implementation existed; and for announcements of this shape, read the departing party's timeline rather than the acquiring party's strategy narrative.
  - Key topics: Deno, Deno Deploy, Deno runtime, Cloudflare, Workers, Durable Objects, celld, workerd, rusty_v8, JSR, Ryan Dahl, Kenton Varda, Bert Belder, SQLite, LTX, Litestream, V8, Tokio, self-hosting, vendor lock-in, open source sustainability, Shopify, Workers for Platforms, acquisition, Hacker News, Simon Willison, 译文

- [Snapdragon X 笔记本的 Linux HDR 支持来了：静态 HDR10，补丁是 LLM 辅助写的](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_qualcomm-msm-drm-hdr/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's report that Qualcomm's MSM DRM kernel driver is gaining static HDR support for DisplayPort outputs and eDP panels, benefiting Snapdragon X laptops running Linux. - [ext4 弃用 data=journal：最「安全」的那个挂载模式，2028 年要走了](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_ext4-deprecates-data-journal/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's report that ext4 has deprecated its journaled data=journal mount mode, merged during the Linux 7.3 merge window (commit 6c377d19d4a5116d9bec5203aa3c6c11523e7898) with removal planned for 2028, after the 2027 Linux LTS kernel. Explains what the mode does (all file data and metadata written to the journal before being committed to the main filesystem, so the journal can be replayed to recover data after a crash or power loss), why it was chosen (it suits users very concerned about data integrity and safety) and its costs as stated in the coverage: significant write performance penalties versus the default data=ordered or data=writeback, plus delayed allocation and Direct I/O support being disabled - the latter mattering for databases and virtual machine images that depend on bypassing the page cache. Adds the three-mode comparison from the kernel documentation: writeback journals no data at all and can leave incorrect data in recently written files after a crash but typically performs best; ordered (the default) journals only metadata yet logically groups data-related metadata with the data blocks in one transaction and writes the associated data blocks first, performing slightly slower than writeback but significantly faster than journal; and journal providing full data and metadata journaling. Notes the documentation's explicit framing that the default mode does not guarantee file data blocks are in any consistent state after a crash, which is precisely the question data=journal answers, and covers fast commits in data=ordered mode storing only the minimal delta needed to recreate affected metadata in space shared with JBD2, which helps explain why the default holds up. Then the supplementary operations section: why the deprecation is technically reasonable (very few users paying for special-case paths in a hot subsystem, with consistency increasingly handled above the filesystem by database WAL and fsync semantics, copy-on-write filesystems using checksums and transactions, and application-level idempotency and replay, while double-writing all data became a poor trade on NVMe where write amplification affects both endurance and performance), and what administrators should do: inventory data=journal across /etc/fstab, systemd mount units, configuration management templates and /proc/mounts; judge whether it is still necessary, since the original reason may no longer exist; evaluate real alternatives rather than blindly switching to data=ordered; and treat the roughly two-year window as a real deadline aligned with distribution upgrades or hardware refreshes. Warns against assuming deprecation requires no action, since the typical path is kernel warnings, then tightened distribution configurations, then a mount failure in 2028 - making a forgotten fstab option a potential boot-time incident, and noting that a mount option sleeping in fstab for a decade suggests the system's configuration was never genuinely reviewed.
  - Key topics: ext4, filesystem, Linux kernel, data=journal, data=ordered, data=writeback, journaling, jbd2, fast commits, delayed allocation, Direct I/O, O_DIRECT, write amplification, data integrity, crash consistency, fsync, write-ahead log, copy-on-write filesystem, Btrfs, ZFS, NVMe, SSD endurance, deprecation, Linux 7.3, Linux LTS 2027, fstab, mount options, operations, Phoronix, 译文

- [Linux swap 子系统要删掉那张「交换映射表」：省下的是 1TB 交换文件里的 256MB](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_linux-swap-table-removing-swap-map/): Translation+analysis of Jonathan Corbet's LWN article on Kairui Song's modernisation of the Linux swap subsystem, the second in a series. Explains the target: the swap map, defined as an unsigned char array with one byte per slot storing the reference count, where the complications live in bit allocation - bit six (0x40) is SWAP_HAS_CACHE marking that a slot has a page assigned, 0x3f is SWAP_MAP_BAD for bad storage, and the resulting maximum reference count is 62 (SWAP_MAP_MAX). Notes that SWAP_HAS_CACHE doubles as a bit lock, with the thread that succeeds in setting it proceeding, which produced delay-and-retry loops and years of bugs; and describes the baroque overflow design (set 0x80 COUNT_CONTINUED, zero the count, allocate a new page supplying eight more significant bits, link it via the LRU list head in the associated page structures, and repeat on further overflow) while preserving the article's point that the motivation for this design is documented nowhere. Covers the first preparatory change, removing the swap bypass added by Minchan Kim in 4.15 (with SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO set and a reference count of one, swap-in happens synchronously with no readahead and the page is not added to the swap cache) on the grounds that the swap table made swap-cache operations fast enough that bypassing it has no real value, that readahead control is now separated and essentially disabled for fast devices, and that all swap I/O through the swap cache simplifies code and reduces race conditions - with the notable functional side effect that large multi-page folios can previously only be swapped in intact when the reference count was one, so removing bypass lifts that restriction. Then the second change, deleting SWAP_HAS_CACHE once the swap cache owns concurrency management and the remaining purpose of marking allocated-but-zero-reference slots is eliminated on both the swap-out side (folio added to the swap cache immediately on slot assignment) and the swap-in side (zero-reference slots freed immediately on removal). Documents the end goal of phase three, eliminating the swap map entirely by moving reference counting into the swap table with a five-way entry format (zero for empty; bit zero set for a shadow entry with the count in the upper bits; bottom two bits 10 for a resident folio storing the page-frame number rather than the address to make room for the count; bottom three bits 100 for a pointer entry, unused in this series; bottom four bits 1000 for a bad slot), the resulting savings (about 30 percent of the subsystem's metadata overhead gone, 256 MB saved for a 1 TB swap file, and the unification of swap map and swap cache), the larger counts available (x86_64 needs 40 bits for the PFN plus two for the resident marker, leaving 22 bits) and the simpler overflow handling (the complex multi-level mechanism removed in favour of allocating an array of unsigned long counts for the entire cluster). Notes the progress state as of the original February 2026 writing (phase two in mm-unstable and linux-next, possibly merged for 7.0; phase three in second revision with little review feedback) and the planned continuation into cgroup swap limits, plus a caution that the article predates the current 7.3 mainline. Closes with why it matters: debt repaid in the right order (bypass removable because swap cache got faster, SWAP_HAS_CACHE removable because the intermediate state was eliminated, swap map removable because its last function found a new home), the shift in swap's assumptions now that memory compression schemes like zram and faster media mean swap I/O is no longer slow and readahead can hurt.
  - Key topics: Linux kernel, swap, memory management, swap map, swap table, swap cluster, SWAP_HAS_CACHE, COUNT_CONTINUED, SWAP_MAP_BAD, SWAP_MAP_MAX, swap bypass, SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO, readahead, swap cache, folio, large folios, page-frame number, shadow entry, Kairui Song, Tencent, mm-unstable, linux-next, Linux 7.0, cgroup swap limits, zram, LWN, Jonathan Corbet, 译文

- [「Linux 桌面永远成功不了」这句话，2026 年该改口了：但作者抱怨的那些事是真的](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_linux-desktop-not-expecting-experts/): Analysis and partial rebuttal of a LinuxLinks opinion piece arguing that Linux will never succeed on the desktop until it stops expecting users to be experts. Agrees with the central argument - that the community applies an odd test where being unable to repair a broken package, parse a terminal error or name your graphics session means Linux is not for you, which comes across as a daft way to promote an operating system - and preserves its strongest material: the analogy that nobody proudly announces their washing machine only works if you can interpret diagnostic codes and edit a configuration file; the separation of capability from needless complication (a capable terminal is a strength and nobody sensible proposes removing it, but trouble starts when command-line workarounds substitute for fixing rough edges in the graphical experience); the refusal to make Linux a pale imitation of Windows; and the formulation that a computer should reward curiosity without demanding it, so you should not have to muck about with the plumbing just to print a document. Highlights the author's own example as the strongest evidence, since he has used Linux for years yet spent far too long on blurry screenshots caused by fractional scaling on a 4K monitor, which reframes the issue from a user-competence problem to a product defect. Then disagrees with the headline using 2026 data: Statcounter puts Linux at 8.88 percent of the global desktop market (September), up from 7.53 percent in July and 5.59 percent in June, with 10.65 percent in North America, 18.19 percent in the United States (up from just over 10 percent in early August) and 7.78 percent in Japan, while Valve's Steam survey shows Linux at 3.90 percent overall and, within Linux, SteamOS Holo at 22.83 percent, CachyOS at 14.03 percent and Bazzite at 7.28 percent, with CachyOS topping DistroWatch's twelve-month hit ranking. Notes the measurement caveats (bots accounted for 23.44 percent of traffic in Statcounter's sample and are removed from the main statistics, and Valve's survey is opt-in) and the irony that the growth is driven by Valve and Steam Deck, an environment where users need not know their graphics session or repair packages. Identifies the gap the article does not address: who pays for 'not requiring experts', since OpenTWEAK-style edge cases such as 4K fractional scaling are fixed by sustained paid engineering, which is why Steam Deck, RHEL and Ubuntu LTS desktops fare better while consumer community distributions lack a funding model for unglamorous work. Closes with the argument that the problem is not community attitude but incentives, and that Valve has demonstrated the viable path.
  - Key topics: Linux desktop, usability, expert expectations, terminal, GNOME, KDE Plasma, fractional scaling, 4K monitor, Steam Deck, SteamOS, CachyOS, Bazzite, Statcounter market share, Valve Steam Hardware Survey, DistroWatch, Linux adoption, funding models, paid engineering, LinuxLinks, 原创

- [452 倍是真的，但它在等一块还不存在的内存条：Meta 的 CRAM 提案](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_meta-cram-compressed-ram/): Analysis of Meta engineer Gregory Price's Compressed RAM (CRAM) presentation at the Linux Plumbers Conference 2026 in Prague on 5 October, reported by Phoronix and Tom's Hardware. Explains the architectural difference from zram and zswap: zram used as swap and zswap both require handling a page fault and decompressing into a regular memory page, while CRAM assumes hardware able to access compressed memory directly at cache-line or byte granularity, leaving compressed pages in the page table so reads never need a decompression target page and no software decompression routine runs. Covers the exposure model (a private NUMA node rather than a simulated block device, so existing memory management machinery such as migration, reclaim, demotion and ballooning continues to work) and disambiguates the name from an unrelated 2010 data-structure paper, a 2018 memory-controller hardware design, and the cramfs filesystem. Presents the read-only benchmark figures from slide 11 with ratios computed (321 vs 325 M ops/s for Zipf 0.99 skewed access and 489 vs 498 M ops/s for uniform random, giving roughly 98.8 and 98.2 percent of DRAM throughput) against zram at around 1.1 M ops/s, which yields the 452x figure in the coverage (489 divided by 1.1 is about 444). Then applies three qualifications: it is a pure-read result, with write rates of 2 percent and 20 percent in uniform random tests dropping CRAM's advantage over zram from about 37x to about 5.4x because compressed pages cannot be modified in place and writes fault the page back to a native node; in the skewed tests zram was terminated by out-of-memory conditions at 10 and 20 percent write rates, so those comparisons are not equivalent; and most importantly the presentation itself annotates that all measurements used DRAM to isolate the cost of page-fault handling, so they should not be read as product benchmarks for the compression hardware's speed or any power-saving claim. Details the three capacity-control mechanisms that prevent the OS from believing it has capacity the hardware cannot hold: pages moved into CRAM are mapped read-only so a write triggers a fault and returns the page to regular DRAM; the entry path is restricted to memory reclaim with CRAM as a private NUMA node excluded from normal allocation; and ballooning, where the driver reports the compression ratio it actually achieves, reserves memory accordingly, and can stop accepting new pages. Covers the hardware barrier - CRAM needs memory hardware capable of real-time decompression with cache-line access, which does not exist on ordinary hardware, making it more likely to land first on CXL memory-tier solutions such as hardware-accelerated compression engines - alongside Phoronix's observation that most individual components needed to support CRAM are already mainline, meaning the software parts are largely in place while the hardware is the missing piece. Closes by situating the work against ongoing zram and zswap improvements (including Qihoo 360's QPaCE driver code for zram and zswap writeback batching patches) and arguing the prototype's value is proving that hardware access to compressed pages can eliminate the entire software decompression path, while the 452x framing is misleading because it combines a read-only result, a same-hardware comparison, and an author-declared non-product benchmark.
  - Key topics: CRAM, Compressed RAM, Meta, Gregory Price, Linux Plumbers Conference 2026, LPC Prague, zram, zswap, swap bypass, memory compression, page fault, page table, folio, NUMA node, ballooning, memory reclaim, cache-line access, hardware decompression, CXL, ZeroPoint Technologies, memory tiering, capacity illusion, compression ratio, TaiChi, 译文

Flags the uncertain details honestly - the 'B' in SB1 may indicate a BGA package but that is explicitly a guess based on the name with no official basis, and the SB1-4U-ACTIVE cooler's maximum power is marked TBD while its 128.05 x 106.6 x 130.7 mm dimensions are identical to Dynatron's J26 cooler for SP7, suggesting placeholder specs. Lists the reported specifications (EPYC 9006 series Verano, up to 72 Zen 6 cores at up to 5 GHz, 24-channel LPDDR5X using replaceable SOCAMM2 modules, a new SB1 socket smaller than SP7 and SP8 requiring different cooling, Dynatron's vapour chamber plus heat pipes and dual ball-bearing fan up to 6,000 RPM, and a second-half 2027 launch). Then argues the real signal is the memory subsystem, supported by three independent strands: ServeTheHome's September coverage of EPYC 9006 Venice already stated AMD would bring 'an AI-focused chip with LPDDR support, a first for an AMD EPYC processor' later in 2027; AMD's own EPYC 9006 product page already organises a 'Host Node for AI' category containing an 'AMD EPYC 9006 LP Server CPU' where LP strongly suggests low power (explicitly framed as the author's inference, not official); and JEDEC's JESD328 SOCAMM2 standard, previewed October 2025 and published June 2026, defines a serviceable LPDDR5X module for data centre AI with data rates up to 9.6 Gb/s per pin, with Rambus shipping a companion chipset (SPD hub plus 12 A and 3 A regulators) since April 2026. Includes a bandwidth estimate labelled as the author's own calculation with its assumptions stated (24 channels at 9.6 Gb/s gives roughly 0.92 TB/s at 32-bit lanes or 1.8 TB/s at 64-bit lanes, against about 614 GB/s for Turin's 12-channel DDR5-6400), concluding the order of magnitude moves toward the low end of HBM. Explains the motivation for LPDDR in servers (DDR5 RDIMM/MRDIMM offers capacity and serviceability at higher energy cost per bit, while LPDDR offers low-voltage efficiency but was historically unsolderable and unserviceable; AI host nodes need bandwidth per watt rather than terabyte capacities, and ServeTheHome noted many workloads do not need anywhere near 1 TB even though that appears to be the floor for 32 channels of 12800 MRDIMM). Closes with procurement implications (SB1 needs new platform and cooling planning, SOCAMM2 makes memory a new form-factor purchase with SPD telemetry to integrate, the story is a roadmap signal rather than a purchasing basis given 2027 timing and TBD part numbers, and capacity-versus-bandwidth node classes may need separate scheduling labels) and the judgement that the 72 cores are unremarkable while the memory change shows AMD defining a distinct AI host CPU category, addressing the memory wall, and doing so on an open JEDEC standard that competitors can follow.
